mainEntity.name: Can a small cavity heal on its own without treatment?

acceptedAnswer.text: Once a physical cavity has formed in the tooth — meaning the enamel surface has broken down — it cannot repair itself naturally. Very early enamel demineralisation (a pre-cavity white spot) may sometimes be reversed with fluoride and excellent oral hygiene, but an actual cavity requires professional treatment. The longer a cavity is left, the deeper it tends to become. Your dentist can assess whether the decay is at a stage where intervention is needed and recommend the most appropriate approach based on a clinical examination.

mainEntity.name: How long does it take for a small cavity to become a root canal?

acceptedAnswer.text: The timeframe varies considerably between individuals and depends on factors such as oral hygiene habits, diet, saliva composition, and the location of the cavity. In some cases, decay can progress from a small cavity to pulp involvement within several months; in others, it may take longer. There is no predictable timeline, which is why regular dental monitoring is valuable. A cavity that appears stable at one appointment may have progressed significantly by the next if left untreated.

mainEntity.name: Does a cavity always cause pain before it needs a root canal?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily. Many patients are surprised to learn that significant decay can develop without any noticeable pain. The tooth's nerve may not produce symptoms until the decay is quite advanced. In some cases, the first sign of a problem is a sudden, severe toothache — by which point the pulp may already be compromised. This is one of the key reasons why routine dental check-ups are so important: they allow detection of decay before symptoms develop, when treatment options are typically simpler.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a filling and a root canal?

acceptedAnswer.text: A filling addresses decay that has not yet reached the tooth's pulp. The decayed material is removed, and the resulting space is filled with a restorative material. A root canal is needed when decay or infection has reached the pulp chamber inside the tooth. During root canal treatment, the infected or inflamed pulp tissue is removed, the internal canals are cleaned and shaped, and the tooth is sealed. A crown may be recommended afterwards to protect the treated tooth. Both are common dental procedures, but a filling is generally quicker and less complex.

Root canal treatment has a reputation that is often worse than the reality. Modern techniques, effective local anaesthesia, and advanced equipment mean that most patients experience little or no discomfort during the procedure. Many patients report that the experience is comparable to having a filling placed. Some mild tenderness after treatment is normal and usually resolves within a few days. If you have concerns about comfort during any dental procedure, discuss this with your dentist beforehand so that appropriate measures can be put in place.

mainEntity.name: How often should I have a dental check-up to catch cavities early?

acceptedAnswer.text: The recommended frequency of dental examinations varies depending on your individual oral health. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) suggests intervals ranging from 3 months to 24 months, based on clinical risk factors. Your dentist will recommend an appropriate schedule after assessing your teeth, gums, and overall oral health. Patients with a higher risk of decay — for example, those with a history of frequent cavities — may benefit from more frequent visits. Regular attendance is one of the most reliable ways to identify and address problems early.
